{{Short description|Mathematical function}}
'''''K''-convex functions''', first introduced by [[Herbert Scarf|Scarf]],<ref name=Scarf>{{cite book|last1=Scarf|first1=H.|title=The Optimality of (S, s) Policies in the Dynamic Inventory Problem|date=1960|publisher=Stanford University Press|location=Stanford, CA|page=Chapter 13}}</ref> are a special weakening of the concept of [[convex function]] which is crucial in the proof of the [[Mathematical optimization|optimality]] of the <math>(s,S)</math> policy in [[Inventory theory|inventory control theory]]. The policy is characterized by two numbers {{mvar|s}} and {{mvar|S}}, <math>S \geq s</math>, such that when the inventory level falls below level {{mvar|s}}, an order is issued for a quantity that brings the inventory up to level {{mvar|S}}, and nothing is ordered otherwise. Gallego and Sethi <ref name="sethigallego">Gallego, G. and Sethi, S. P. (2005). ''K''-convexity in ℜ<sup>n</sup>. ''Journal of Optimization Theory & Applications,'' 127(1):71-88.</ref> have generalized the concept of ''K''-convexity to higher dimensional Euclidean spaces.

== Definition ==
Two equivalent definitions are as follows:

=== Definition 1 (The original definition) ===
Let ''K'' be a non-negative real number. A function <math>g: \mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</math> is ''K''-convex if
:<math>g(u)+z\left[\frac{g(u)-g(u-b)}{b}\right] \leq g(u+z) + K</math>
for any <math>u, z\geq 0,</math> and <math>b>0</math>.

=== Definition 2  (Definition with geometric interpretation) ===
A function <math>g: \mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</math> is ''K''-convex if
:<math>g(\lambda x+\bar{\lambda} y) \leq \lambda g(x) + \bar{\lambda} [g(y)+K]</math>
for all <math>x\leq y, \lambda \in [0,1]</math>, where <math>\bar{\lambda}=1-\lambda</math>.

This definition admits a simple geometric interpretation related to the concept of visibility.<ref name=Kolmogorov>{{cite book|last1=Kolmogorov|first1=A. N.|last2=Fomin|first2=S. V.|author-link=Andrey Kolmogorov|author-link2=Sergei Fomin|title=Introduction to Real Analysis|date=1970|publisher=Dover Publications Inc.|location=New York}}</ref> Let <math>a \geq 0</math>. A point <math>(x,f(x))</math> is said to be visible from <math>(y,f(y)+a)</math> if all intermediate points <math>(\lambda x+\bar{\lambda} y, f(\lambda x+\bar{\lambda} y)), 0\leq \lambda \leq 1</math> lie below the line segment joining these two points. Then the geometric characterization of ''K''-convexity can be obtain as:

:A function <math>g</math> is ''K''-convex if and only if <math>(x,g(x))</math> is visible from <math>(y,g(y)+K)</math> for all <math>y\geq x</math>.

=== Proof of equivalence ===
It is sufficient to prove that the above definitions can be transformed to each other. This can be seen by using the transformation
:<math> \lambda = z/(b+z),\quad x=u-b,\quad y=u+z.</math>

== Properties == 
<ref>Sethi S P, Cheng F. Optimality of (s, S) Policies in Inventory Models with Markovian Demand. INFORMS, 1997.</ref>

=== Property 1 ===
If <math>g: \mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</math> is ''K''-convex, then it is ''L''-convex for any <math>L\geq K</math>. In particular, if <math>g</math> is convex, then it is also ''K''-convex for any <math>K\geq 0</math>.

=== Property 2 ===
If <math>g_1</math> is ''K''-convex and <math>g_2</math> is ''L''-convex, then for <math>\alpha \geq 0, \beta \geq 0,\; g=\alpha g_1 +\beta g_2</math> is <math>(\alpha K+\beta L)</math>-convex.

=== Property 3 ===
If <math>g</math> is ''K''-convex and <math>\xi</math> is a random variable such that <math>E|g(x-\xi)|<\infty</math> for all <math>x</math>, then <math>Eg(x-\xi)</math> is also ''K''-convex.

=== Property 4 ===
If <math>g: \mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</math> is ''K''-convex, restriction of <math>g</math> on any convex set <math>\mathbb{D}\subset\mathbb{R}</math> is ''K''-convex.

=== Property 5 ===
If <math>g: \mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</math> is a continuous ''K''-convex function and <math>g(y)\rightarrow \infty</math> as <math>|y|\rightarrow \infty</math>, then there exit scalars <math>s</math> and <math>S</math> with <math>s\leq S</math> such that
* <math>g(S)\leq g(y)</math>, for all <math>y\in \mathbb{R}</math>;
* <math>g(S)+K=g(s)<g(y)</math>, for all <math>y<s</math>;
* <math>g(y)</math> is a decreasing function on <math>(-\infty, s)</math>;
* <math>g(y)\leq g(z)+K</math> for all <math>y, z</math> with <math>s\leq y\leq z</math>.
